name: 5:2 diet / alternate-day fasting

lead: The 5:2 diet restricts intake to roughly 500 to 600 calories on two non-consecutive days and eats normally on the other five. Alternate-day fasting alternates very low-calorie days with normal days. People use both to build a weekly calorie deficit and lower body fat for a leaner look.

The low days cut weekly intake, so fat and some lean mass are lost. Reviews report weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent in most human studies, comparable to continuous calorie restriction, and reviews suggest exercise to help retain lean mass.

paras: Followers pick two fast days a week (5:2) or fast every other day, eating normally in between. Many pair it with resistance training to keep muscle. Results build over weeks as the weekly deficit accumulates.

Hunger, irritability, dizziness and headaches are common early on. Health bodies say it is not recommended for pregnancy, children, adolescents, older adults, underweight people or those with eating disorders.

angle.text: Very low-calorie fast days create a weekly calorie deficit that lowers body fat and gives a leaner look. Trials show weight loss comparable to ordinary dieting, and appearance outcomes themselves have not been studied.

lead: The 5:2 diet and alternate-day fasting are two forms of intermittent energy restriction. The 5:2 pattern has two non-consecutive days of roughly 500 to 600 calories and normal eating on the other five; alternate-day fasting alternates a very low-calorie day (under about 25 percent of usual needs) with a normal "feast" day, and a modified version allows up to 25 percent of calories on fast days.[1]

Documented in a 2011 article by Harvie and colleagues, the 5:2 diet was popularized in the UK and Australia by Michael Mosley through the 2012 BBC Horizon documentary Eat, Fast and Live Longer.[1] Reviews report weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent in most human studies, with limited evidence that it outperforms continuous calorie restriction.[1]
infobox: Two non-consecutive low-calorie days (about 500-600 kcal) per week
Fast day alternating with normal-eating day

paras: Both protocols are grouped with time-restricted eating under intermittent fasting, all involving alternating periods of fasting and ad libitum eating.[2] Periodic or whole-day fasting with water only is a separate category.[1]

A 2024 umbrella review found improvements in waist circumference, fat mass, LDL cholesterol, triglycerides and fasting insulin with intermittent fasting, with a smaller blood-pressure benefit than continuous calorie restriction.[1] A 2021 review reported that moderate alternate-day fasting for 2 to 6 months reduced weight, BMI and cardiometabolic risk factors.[1] A Cochrane review found it uncertain whether intermittent fasting prevents cardiovascular disease.[1]

Like other diets, intermittent fasting typically induces loss of both fat and lean mass, and a 2025 narrative review proposes exercise as an adjunct to retain lean mass.[2] A review on women's health discusses intermittent energy restriction in women with overweight and with healthy weight, noting reduced adherence to daily restriction as a reason for developing intermittent regimens.[3] Reported dropout rates were 2 to 38 percent for intermittent fasting versus 0 to 50 percent for calorie restriction.[1]

Short-term effects include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired thinking, which usually fade within a month.[1] It is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and adolescents, older adults, underweight people, or those with or at risk of eating disorders.[1]

The US National Institute on Aging says research is limited and inconclusive and does not recommend these diets for the general public; the American Heart Association says there is no good evidence of heart-health benefits; the UK NHS advises people considering 5:2 to consult a physician first.[1]

timeline.event: Harvie and colleagues document the 5:2 diet.[1]
